nodes.title: Terraform variables and locals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Terraform input variables make configurations reusable; locals simplify repeated expressions. The TF-003 exam heavily tests type constraints, validation blocks, sensitive flags, and the precedence order for variable assignment.

flashcards.front: Five ways to assign a Terraform variable (highest to lowest precedence)?
flashcards.back: -var flag > -var-file flag > *.auto.tfvars (alphabetical) > terraform.tfvars > TF_VAR_name env var. Higher-precedence sources override lower ones.

flashcards.front: What does sensitive = true do on a variable?
flashcards.back: Redacts the value from CLI output and plan display. It does NOT encrypt the value in state — state still stores it in plaintext, so the backend must be secured separately.

flashcards.front: When to use locals vs variable?
flashcards.back: Use locals for computed or repeated expressions internal to a module that callers should not override (e.g. a concatenated name). Use variables for values callers should supply. Locals cannot be set from outside the module.

flashcards.front: Type constraint any vs object({ ... }) — trade-offs?
flashcards.back: object({ key = type }) enforces a specific schema with required keys and types — prefer this for safety. any disables type checking entirely and should only be used for dynamic wrapper modules where the type is intentionally unknown.

questions.q: A Bash loop `for f in *.log; do gzip $f; done` fails on filenames that contain spaces. Which fix quotes the variable so gzip sees each filename as a single argument?
choices: `for f in *.log; do gzip ${f}; done` — brace form; still unquoted, so word-splitting on spaces remains
`for f in "*.log"; do gzip $f; done` — quotes prevent GLOB expansion; the literal string `*.log` becomes the only iterated value
`for f in *.log; do gzip '$f'; done` — single quotes pass the literal characters `$f` to gzip, not the variable value
`for f in *.log; do gzip "$f"; done` — double-quoted expansion keeps each filename (spaces included) as one shell word
questions.explanation: Only `"$f"` (double-quoted parameter expansion) protects filenames with spaces from being split into multiple arguments. `${f}` clarifies where the variable name ends but still expands unquoted, so word-splitting kicks in. `"*.log"` prevents glob expansion — the loop iterates the LITERAL string `*.log` once, not the matching files. `'$f'` passes the literal three-character string `$f` to gzip; single quotes suppress variable expansion entirely.

questions.q: A Bash script exits with status code 127. What does exit code 127 specifically mean in Bash?
choices: `Command not found` — Bash could not locate the requested executable in PATH (typo or missing binary)
`Permission denied` — Bash found the executable but the user lacks execute permission (exit 126 is the actual code for that)
`Segmentation fault` — a SIGSEGV kill produces status 139 (128+11), not 127
Successful exit — status 0 signals success; non-zero always signals an error
questions.explanation: In Bash, 127 is the well-defined status for `command not found` — typo in the command name, missing binary, or wrong PATH. `Permission denied on an executable file` is 126 (found but not executable). A segfault is reported as 128 + signal number = 139 for SIGSEGV, not 127. Exit code 0 means success by convention; anything non-zero means an error, but the specific code 127 always means "not found".

questions.q: A Bash script must check that `/var/log/app.log` exists AND is a regular file (not a directory, symlink target that vanished, socket, or block device) before it reads from it. Which conditional test fits?
choices: `[ -x /var/log/app.log ]` — tests EXECUTABILITY, unrelated to file-type filtering
`[ -e /var/log/app.log ]` — tests EXISTENCE but does not distinguish regular files from directories/sockets/devices
`[ -d /var/log/app.log ]` — tests for a DIRECTORY, which is the opposite of what we want
`[ -f /var/log/app.log ]` — tests that the path exists AND that stat() reports it as a regular file
questions.explanation: `[ -f PATH ]` is the classical regular-file predicate: it returns true if the path both exists AND `stat()` reports it as a regular file (mode `S_IFREG`). `[ -e PATH ]` is the pure existence check and does not filter by type — directories, sockets, char/block devices and FIFOs all pass. `[ -d PATH ]` is the directory predicate — the opposite of what the scenario needs. `[ -x PATH ]` checks the effective UID has execute permission; it has nothing to do with file type filtering. (For symlinks, `-f` follows the link and returns true only if the target is a regular file, which is usually what a log-reading script wants.)

questions.q: A Bash function `check_connectivity` returns 0 on success or 1 on failure. What is the correct way to CAPTURE that return code into a shell variable?
choices: `result=check_connectivity()` — Bash treats this as an ASSIGNMENT of the literal string `check_connectivity()`, the function is not run
`check_connectivity; result=$?` — runs the function and then reads `$?`, which holds the exit status of the last command
`result=$(check_connectivity)` — captures STDOUT, not the exit code; `result` ends up with any text the function printed
`export result; check_connectivity` — declares `result` as an environment variable before the function runs; nothing writes to it
questions.explanation: `$?` is Bash's built-in variable holding the exit status of the last foreground command or function, so `check_connectivity; result=$?` runs the function and captures its return code. `result=check_connectivity()` is not a call at all — Bash sees a variable assignment of a literal string with `()` glued on and never invokes the function. `result=$(check_connectivity)` runs the function in a subshell and captures its STDOUT, so `result` holds any echoed text rather than the exit code. `export result; check_connectivity` merely marks `result` for export; nothing writes to it.

questions.q: A bash script fails intermittently in production. To debug, the administrator wants to see every command EXECUTED with variables expanded and prefixed with `+`. Which invocation enables that trace mode?
choices: `bash -e script.sh` — enables errexit so the script aborts on the FIRST command that returns non-zero; useful as a safety belt but prints no trace of what ran
`bash -v script.sh` — echoes each raw source line to stderr as it is READ from disk (before variable expansion), so you see the code but not the runtime values
`bash -x script.sh` — enables xtrace: every command is echoed to stderr prefixed with `+` after parameter expansion but before execution, so you see actual values
`bash -n script.sh` — enables noexec; the shell parses the script and reports any syntax error but never actually runs a command from it (dry-run parse)
questions.explanation: `bash -x` enables xtrace: each command is printed to stderr with a `+ ` prefix AFTER parameter and command substitution but BEFORE execution, so the actual expanded values are visible. `bash -v` prints the RAW source lines as they are read — helpful for parse errors but shows the unexpanded form. `bash -e` (errexit) aborts on the first failing command and prints nothing extra, so it is a safety mode, not a trace mode. `bash -n` (noexec) walks the syntax and reports parse errors without ever running the script.

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.

questions.q: A sysadmin has written a new systemd service unit `appd.service` and wants `systemctl enable appd` to start the service automatically when the system reaches `multi-user.target`. Which directive belongs in the [Install] section of the unit?
choices: `WantedBy=multi-user.target` — enable creates a symlink in multi-user.target.wants/ so the target pulls it in
`After=multi-user.target` — only orders start-up, no autostart symlink is created
`Requires=multi-user.target` — declares a dependency but does not register the unit with a target
`RequiredBy=multi-user.target` — not a valid [Install] directive on any released systemd version
questions.explanation: `WantedBy=multi-user.target` in the [Install] section is what `systemctl enable` looks for: it creates the symlink `/etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/appd.service`, so when systemd reaches multi-user.target the unit is pulled in and started. `After=` belongs in [Unit] and only orders start-up relative to another unit — it never causes autostart. `Requires=` also belongs in [Unit]; it declares a hard dependency but again does not register the unit with a target for enablement. `RequiredBy=` is not a recognised directive on shipping systemd releases (only `WantedBy=` and `RequiredBy=` documentation confusion — the actual [Install] keys are `WantedBy`, `Also`, `Alias`, `DefaultInstance`).

questions.q: A systemd unit with `Type=forking` fails to start; the journal shows `Timeout waiting for PID file`. What is the MOST likely misconfiguration in the unit file?
choices: The unit's `PIDFile=` directive is missing or points to a path the daemon never writes
`Type=simple` should be used instead — forking mode is deprecated in current systemd releases
The `ExecStart=` binary is missing from disk, which produces this timeout instead of an execve error
`[Install] WantedBy=` is not set, and systemd refuses to start units that are not enabled to a target
questions.explanation: When `Type=forking` is set, systemd starts the initial process, expects it to fork, expects the parent to exit, and then waits for the daemon's PID file to appear so it can track the surviving child. A missing or mistyped `PIDFile=` produces exactly the observed `Timeout waiting for PID file` error. `Type=simple` (not forking) is the systemd-preferred style but is not deprecated — traditional daemons that fork legitimately still need `forking`. A missing ExecStart binary raises `status=203/EXEC` immediately, not a PID-file timeout. `[Install] WantedBy=` only affects whether `systemctl enable` creates a symlink; it does not gate manual starts.

questions.q: After rebooting a system, an administrator notices that a custom service file at `/etc/systemd/system/myapp.service` was edited on disk but systemd still uses the OLD contents. Which command tells systemd to re-read unit files from disk without restarting the service?
choices: `systemctl reset-failed myapp` — clears the FAILED state flag; does not re-read unit files
`systemctl reload myapp` — asks the SERVICE (via SIGHUP or ExecReload=) to reload its own config, not systemd itself
`systemctl daemon-reload` — re-parses every unit file from disk and rebuilds systemd's in-memory dependency graph
`systemctl restart myapp` — restarts the process using systemd's CACHED copy of the old unit file
questions.explanation: `systemctl daemon-reload` is the exact command for this scenario: it re-reads every unit file from disk (including your edited `myapp.service`), rebuilds the dependency graph and applies the new configuration to the systemd manager. `systemctl restart` alone uses the CACHED unit that daemon-reload has not yet refreshed, so the edits are ignored. `systemctl reload` sends the service its own `ExecReload=` (or SIGHUP) so the running daemon rereads ITS config file — not systemd's unit. `reset-failed` only clears the FAILED marker so the next start attempt is allowed; it does not refresh unit files.

questions.q: A systemd service `webapp` shows `Active: failed (Result: exit-code)`. Which command shows the process's own stdout/stderr as captured by systemd so the administrator can see WHY it exited?
choices: `cat /var/log/webapp.log` — assumes the service writes to that file; many modern services log to stdout, which is captured by the journal instead
`dmesg | grep webapp` — dmesg is the kernel ring buffer; it does not contain userspace stdout/stderr
`systemctl show webapp` — prints the unit's PROPERTIES (ExecStart, Restart, etc.) in key=value form; no runtime logs
`journalctl -u webapp -n 100 --no-pager` — pulls the last 100 journal entries for the webapp UNIT, including stdout/stderr that systemd captured
questions.explanation: systemd captures every unit's stdout and stderr into the journal, tagged with the unit name. `journalctl -u webapp -n 100` (or `-e` to jump to the end) is the exact query for a failed unit's own runtime output, including the last few lines that immediately preceded the failure. `systemctl show webapp` prints property key=value pairs (ExecStart, Restart, MainPID) — no log data. `dmesg` is the kernel ring buffer; userspace stdout does not go there. Assuming `/var/log/webapp.log` exists is only correct if the daemon opens that file itself — many packaged services now rely on journald.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A security policy requires that the account `jsmith` be prevented from logging in with a password RIGHT NOW, without deleting the account, its home directory or its data. Which command achieves that?
choices: `chage -I -1 jsmith` — sets password inactivity to -1 which disables the inactivity feature, it does not lock the account
`usermod -L jsmith` — prefixes the /etc/shadow password hash with `!`, so no password can match
`passwd -e jsmith` — expires the password so the user MUST change it on next login, but they can still log in
`userdel -r jsmith` — deletes the user AND their home directory, which the policy explicitly forbids
questions.explanation: `usermod -L jsmith` (equivalent to `passwd -l`) locks the account by prepending `!` to the hash in /etc/shadow, so no supplied password can ever match — the account and its data are untouched. `passwd -e` only marks the password as expired: the user is forced to set a new one on next login but is not actually blocked. `chage -I -1` explicitly disables the inactivity feature, which is the opposite of locking. `userdel -r` removes the user entry AND the home directory, which violates the requirement to keep the data intact.

questions.q: `chage -l alice` prints `Password expires: Mar 01, 2026`. It is now late April 2026 and Alice can still log in with her password. What is the MOST likely reason her expired password is still accepted?
choices: The `INACTIVE` field in /etc/shadow grants a grace period after expiry during which the password still works (with a forced change)
PAM has been reconfigured to ignore /etc/shadow expiry — the default `pam_unix` configuration would normally block her
`chage` reads a different source than /etc/shadow, so the tool's report is out of date compared to the real hash file
SSH public-key authentication bypasses password expiry — even though the scenario says she is entering a password
questions.explanation: The `INACTIVE` field (column 7 in /etc/shadow) sets how many days AFTER the password expiry the account still accepts logins, forcing a password change on entry. Set it to a large value and the user keeps working past the printed expiry date. `pam_unix` on a default system honours shadow expiry, so "PAM ignores expiry" is not the default explanation. `chage` reads /etc/shadow directly, so its report cannot be stale compared to shadow. SSH public-key auth would bypass expiry, but the scenario explicitly says Alice logs in with her password, so keys are not what is happening.

questions.q: After `useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G wheel devuser`, /etc/passwd shows devuser's PRIMARY group as `devuser`, not `wheel`. Why?
choices: The wheel group is missing on this box, so useradd silently fell back to a default private group
`-G` sets the primary group, so useradd overrode it with the passwd defaults from /etc/login.defs
`-m` implies primary-group creation and takes precedence over any group flag on the same command line
`useradd` creates a user-private primary group named after the user by default; `-G wheel` only adds wheel as a SUPPLEMENTARY group
questions.explanation: By default (`USERGROUPS_ENAB yes` in /etc/login.defs), `useradd` creates a private group named after the user and makes it the primary group. `-G` is exclusively for SUPPLEMENTARY groups; the primary is set with lowercase `-g`. If `wheel` did NOT exist, useradd would fail with an error rather than fall back silently — so option A is wrong. `-m` controls whether the home directory is created and copied from /etc/skel; it does not touch group assignment. So `devuser` is the primary group, and `wheel` is a supplementary group as requested.

questions.q: On a UEFI-booted system running GRUB2, the administrator wants to change the boot-menu timeout so the user has more time to pick an older kernel entry. Which file should they edit and then regenerate grub.cfg from?
choices: `/boot/grub2/grub.cfg` — the compiled menu; editing it directly is overwritten on the next grub2-mkconfig
`/etc/grub.d/40_custom` — for adding CUSTOM menu entries, not for changing global settings like the timeout
`/boot/grub2/grubenv` — a key/value environment file that stores `saved_entry`, not the timeout
`/etc/default/grub` — holds `GRUB_TIMEOUT=` and friends, consumed by grub2-mkconfig when it rebuilds grub.cfg
questions.explanation: `/etc/default/grub` is where you set `GRUB_TIMEOUT=`, `GRUB_DEFAULT=`, `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX=` and similar knobs; `grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` then bakes them into the actual menu. `/boot/grub2/grub.cfg` IS the compiled menu and is stamped as auto-generated — hand edits are wiped on the next `grub2-mkconfig` run. `/etc/grub.d/40_custom` is the drop-in for hand-authored menu entries (rescue images, extra distros); it does not hold the timeout. `/boot/grub2/grubenv` is a small block-aligned env file that stores runtime state such as `saved_entry`, not menu configuration.

questions.q: GRUB2 dropped the system to the `grub rescue>` prompt. `ls` reports `(hd0) (hd0,gpt1) (hd0,gpt2)`, where /boot lives on `(hd0,gpt2)`. Which sequence of commands boots the running system to userspace?
choices: `insmod normal` then `normal` — that only works from the FULL GRUB shell once modules load; from `grub rescue>` you need the rescue-mode sequence
`grub-install (hd0); update-grub; boot` — `grub-install` and `update-grub` require a booted OS and cannot run from the rescue prompt
`boot (hd0,gpt2)/vmlinuz root=/dev/sda2` — GRUB rescue has no `boot IMAGE` form; you must first set root, load linux and initrd, then run boot
`set prefix=(hd0,gpt2)/grub2; set root=(hd0,gpt2); insmod normal; normal` — sets prefix/root, loads the normal module, then hands off to the standard GRUB menu
questions.explanation: From `grub rescue>` the rescue shell only has a tiny built-in command set; the recovery pattern is to tell it where GRUB's modules live (`set prefix=(hd0,gpt2)/grub2`), set root, then load `insmod normal` and enter normal mode, which finds grub.cfg and boots as usual. Option A skips the required prefix/root setup and cannot find `normal.mod` on its own. Option B calls tools (`grub-install`, `update-grub`) that need a running Linux userspace — you are trying to get there. Option C uses a syntax `boot IMAGE` that GRUB2 does not accept; the correct hand-boot sequence is `linux ...; initrd ...; boot` — a single `boot IMAGE` line is not valid.

questions.q: A production system's GRUB2 menu has two kernel entries. The administrator edits `/etc/default/grub` and sets `GRUB_DEFAULT=0` so the newer kernel becomes the default. What must be run for the change to take effect?
choices: `grub2-install /dev/sda` — reinstalls the bootloader to the MBR; does not rebuild grub.cfg from /etc/default/grub
`systemctl reboot` — reboots the machine but reads the OLD grub.cfg because it was never regenerated
`grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` — rebuilds grub.cfg from /etc/default/grub and /etc/grub.d/*, applying the new setting
`update-grub && reboot` — `update-grub` is the Debian/Ubuntu wrapper name; on RHEL/CentOS it is `grub2-mkconfig`
questions.explanation: `grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` (RHEL/CentOS) or `grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg` (some Debian derivatives) reads /etc/default/grub together with the scriptlets in /etc/grub.d/*, and writes a new grub.cfg. That is the step that translates `GRUB_DEFAULT=0` into a real change in the boot menu. `grub2-install` reinstalls the boot loader binary to the disk MBR/EFI partition — not the same as regenerating grub.cfg. `systemctl reboot` would just reboot with the stale grub.cfg. `update-grub` is Debian/Ubuntu's wrapper for grub-mkconfig — the intent is right but the tool is not available on RHEL/CentOS.

questions.q: A developer's script at `/opt/readcert.sh` (owned by root) must read files in `/etc/ssl/private` (root-owned) WITHOUT giving the developer full root access. Which configuration best satisfies least-privilege?
choices: Dedicated group `sslreaders`: add the developer to it, chgrp the key directory to it, set mode 750 on the directory (640 on files inside)
`chmod 4755 /opt/readcert.sh` — set SUID so the script always runs as root; Linux, however, ignores SUID on interpreted scripts as a well-known race-condition mitigation
Add the developer to the `root` group and set `/etc/ssl/private` to 640 — but the root group grants access to root-group-owned files scattered across the entire system, not just SSL keys
`chmod +t /etc/ssl/private` — set the sticky bit on the directory; sticky only prevents non-owners from DELETING files inside, it has no effect at all on read permission
questions.explanation: Least privilege is a dedicated group: create `sslreaders`, add just the developer, change group ownership on `/etc/ssl/private` (and the key files inside it), then `chmod 750` on the directory and `640` on the files. The developer gets exactly the reads they need and nothing else. Setting SUID on a shell script is a common trap — the Linux kernel deliberately ignores the SUID bit on interpreted scripts to close a well-known race window, so `chmod 4755` does nothing useful. Adding a user to the `root` group grants read access to every root-group-owned file on the box, far beyond `/etc/ssl/private`. The sticky bit on a directory only prevents users from deleting files they do not own; it has no effect on read permission.

questions.q: Which numeric-notation `chmod` sets `/opt/script.sh` to `rwxr-x---` (owner rwx, group r-x, other no access)?
choices: `chmod 755 /opt/script.sh` — sets other=r-x (5), granting world execute which the requirement forbids
`chmod 750 /opt/script.sh` — owner=rwx (7), group=r-x (5), other=--- (0), matching the requirement exactly
`chmod 740 /opt/script.sh` — sets group=r-- (4), stripping execute from the group which the requirement requires
`chmod 754 /opt/script.sh` — sets other=r-- (4), granting world read which the requirement forbids
questions.explanation: Decoding `rwxr-x---`: owner rwx=4+2+1=7, group r-x=4+0+1=5, other ---=0, so the mode is `750`. `755` adds r-x for other, which the requirement forbids. `740` strips execute from the group (`r--` = 4). `754` grants read to other (`r--` = 4), also forbidden. Only `750` matches the exact rwx pattern given.
